posts.text: “IT is dead.” No, it’s not. The IT industry of 5 years ago is dead though. I spend my days talking to hundreds of developers, founders, hiring managers. The story that's been dominating the conversation recently is one of AI-induced panic. I've participated in conversations where the veterans are saying they haven't written a line of code in long months, the juniors are saying there's absolutely no point in studying and everyone is planning their exit to go and become an air conditioning installer. Let's just sum up where we are at the moment. 1. Syntax is a commodity. Problem solving is the premium. The candidates who are struggling are the ones who define themselves by writing code. The ones who are getting the jobs (often at a higher rate) are the ones who define themselves by solving problems. AI writes the syntax. Humans own the architecture, the business logic and the accountability. If your only skill is taking a spec and turning it into code then yes, most likely you're in trouble. If your skill is in understanding what needs to be built and why then you're more valuable than ever. 2. The "Junior Gap" is very much a real thing, just not a permanent one. Companies aren't hiring juniors to write CRUD apps anymore. If they hire them, it is mainly to manage AI agents, validate AI output and deal with the integration complexity. The entry level has just moved from "can you code?" to "can you orchestrate technology to deliver business value?" 3. The hybrid roles are exploding. The most in demand profiles at the moment aren't the pure developer. They're DevOps + Security, Product + Engineering, Data + Business Intelligence, etc. The silos are breaking down. What companies are looking for is someone who can speak both the language of the engineer and the language of the stakeholder. The pure coder is being superseded by the technologist who understands the context. To the candidates feeling lost: Don't be comparing yourself to the 2021 benchmark. That market is dead. Your value at the moment isn't in how fast you can type. It's in how good a thinker you are, how much you understand the systems and how effectively you can use tools (particularly AI) to amplify your output. To the founders hiring: Stop filtering for keywords. Start filtering for adaptability, curiosity and problem solving depth. The best engineers today are the ones who can learn any framework and use AI to move 10x faster. Founders & Hiring Managers, what's the change you're seeing, are you hiring any differently in 2026? Share your thoughts below.

posts.text: Apple is hiring Software Engineers in AI. Apple is looking for engineers to join its AI & Data Platforms team in Hyderabad, India, to build AI-powered solutions that solve real business problems at scale. The team works with large-scale enterprise data, generative AI, machine learning, and agentic solutions that support business functions across Retail, Sales, Finance, Operations, Marketing, and more. Key requirements: - Bachelor's degree or equivalent practical experience, with 2+ years in software and applied AI/ML engineering. - Strong programming skills in Python or Java. - Hands-on experience building GenAI applications using RAG pipelines, embeddings, vector databases, and semantic search. - Practical experience building AI agents and agentic workflows involving planning, memory, tool use, and execution. - Ability to integrate structured and unstructured enterprise data into AI-powered applications. Good to have: - Full-stack development experience across backend APIs, data services, and frontend applications. - Experience with AWS, GCP, or Azure, with AWS preferred. - Familiarity with PyTorch or TensorFlow. - Experience building multi-agent systems and taking AI prototypes into production. How to prepare for the interview: 1. Python or Java: Practise data structures, algorithms, complexity analysis, and writing clean, testable code. 2. RAG and vector databases: Understand chunking, embeddings, retrieval strategies, reranking, semantic search, and how to evaluate retrieval quality. 3. AI agents: Be prepared to explain tool calling, planning, memory, execution loops, failure handling, and when an agent is actually necessary. 4. System design: Practise designing a production-grade AI application, including APIs, data pipelines, caching, scalability, security, monitoring, and reliability. 5. Project deep dives: Be ready to explain an AI project you built, the architecture you chose, the trade-offs you made, and how you measured its performance. 6. Production readiness: Understand hallucination reduction, evaluation, observability, governance, latency, and cost optimization. These are preparation recommendations based on the role's requirements, not a confirmed list of Apple's interview rounds. posts.author: Mohd Anas Choudhary
posts.headline: CSE Student | Builder & Problem Solver | Exploring AI × Product × Entrepreneurship
posts.text: The standard playbook for CSE students seems simple: Grind LeetCode. Master algorithms. Build another portfolio project. But the more I explore software development, the more I realize that "solving problems and building software are two different skills." Both matter. They just teach you different things. 1. LeetCode gives you defined problems. Real projects give you unexpected ones. In a coding problem, you usually know the inputs, constraints, and expected output. In a real project, an API fails, authentication breaks, a database query slows down, or a user does something you never anticipated. You have to figure out what's wrong, not just find the optimal solution. 2. Writing a function is different from understanding a system. Solving an algorithmic problem teaches you to think about correctness and efficiency. Building an application teaches you how the frontend, backend, database, authentication, and external services work together — and what happens when one part fails. 3. Passing tests isn't the same as solving a user's problem. Your code can pass every test and still be part of a product nobody wants to use. Real users reveal problems you might never discover by testing your code alone. I'm not saying LeetCode is useless. Data structures, algorithms, and problem-solving fundamentals matter, especially for technical interviews. But I don't want my entire learning journey to revolve around solving isolated problems. I also want to build, ship, debug, and understand what it takes to make software work outside my development environment. My current takeaway: learn the fundamentals, but don't postpone building until you feel ready. For senior engineers, hiring managers, and fellow builders: When you evaluate a junior developer, what matters most beyond their DSA skills — their projects, debugging ability, system understanding, or something else? #SoftwareEngineering #BuildInPublic #ComputerScience #StudentLife #Tech

posts.text: A little belated, but in September, I crossed my 5-year milestone at Luce Maintenance Group. It has been incredible to watch Luce be recognized among Singapore's fastest-growing companies along the way, climbing from rank 79 in 2023 to rank 34 in 2026. I joined just one year into the company's transition from traditional workflows to a modern tech stack. Starting as an Associate on the frontend, my initial focus was building our internal ops dashboard to streamline worker scheduling and improve efficiency. Progressing into a Senior Software Engineer role over the years, my scope naturally expanded into full-stack and product engineering. Taking ownership of our client-facing self-booking platform was a major turning point for the business. The impact was massive. After introducing client-originated bookings, both our average monthly platform volume and package value increased 2.5x. The new client platform drove 99% of this observed uplift. Today, client bookings make up over 60% of our total volume, allowing us to scale and support 15 different service departments. Beyond the codebase, I stepped into leadership. This included mentoring engineers, building an OKR-based product roadmap, collaborating closely with marketing to drive user acquisition, and partnering with HR to shape our engineering hiring process. Lately, my core focus has been stabilizing our shared cross-platform design system in a single monorepo. Alongside this, my scope spans across our broader infrastructure, managing our CI/CD pipelines, system observability, and streamlining our frontend and backend error handling. To push our engineering velocity even further, we built our own AI agent harness, integrating AI directly into our workflow while maintaining a single, unified brand across all platforms. None of this would have been possible without my manager and director, Zhang Yitao. Since my first year, he gave me the opportunity to become a core part of this journey. His guidance in transforming the business, building an agile engineering team that prioritizes product value, and exposing me closely to the business side has been invaluable. 🥂 Cheers to five years of building, scaling, and learning! Onward to the next challenge 💪🏻 #WorkMilestone #WorkAnniversary

posts.headline: Product & Data
posts.text: Are data analyst jobs disappearing? I pulled the numbers instead of guessing. I'm a data engineer looking for my next role, and I kept hearing that AI is wiping out data jobs. So I looked at two datasets: 1. Indeed's public job postings index, by category, 2020 to Oct 2026 2. Every Hacker News "Who is hiring?" thread since 2019: 95 threads, about 49,000 company posts, counted by role What I found: Data & Analytics postings on Indeed are at 64% of their Feb 2020 level. That's the lowest of 47 job categories. All US postings are at 104%. BUT! The fall started before ChatGPT. Data postings peaked in March 2022 and were already down 29% by Nov 2022. Rate hikes and tech cuts started it. AI looks like the reason the category stayed low while software jobs began recovering in 2025. The three roles moved differently. In startup hiring posts: • Data scientist mentions fell from 10.8% of posts to 3.5% • Data engineer mentions held up best, from 6.5% to 4.1% • Data analyst mentions slipped from 1.4% to 0.6% • ML and AI engineer mentions tripled, from 3.4% to 10.2% My takeaway: AI is reshaping data work more than replacing it. Junior, dashboard-only roles are shrinking fastest. Roles that build the data layer (pipelines, models, warehouses) and analysts who know a business domain are holding up much better. Yale Budget Lab and Stanford research point the same way: no broad collapse yet, but early-career roles feel it first. If you're in data, which side are you seeing? Sources: Indeed Hiring Lab job postings tracker, HN Algolia API, BLS Employment Projections 2024 to 34, Yale Budget Lab, Stanford Digital Economy Lab. #DataEngineering #DataAnalytics #JobMarket #AI

posts.text: SaaS gurus are mad at me for saying Enterprise SaaS is dead. 🤦🏽‍♂️ I get it. It’s your bread and butter. But you’d have to be living under a rock to believe businesses will continue paying outrageous subscription fees for enterprise software when cheaper alternatives are becoming increasingly viable. Just yesterday, Anton Osika announced new capabilities for Lovable’s enterprise offering. And this is only the beginning. Enterprises around the world are figuring out how to reduce recurring software costs by: 1. Switching to newer, better, and cheaper SaaS products. 2. Experimenting with AI tools to build software in-house. 3. Hiring external developers like hashpotato equipped with AI tools to build custom alternatives. AI is fundamentally changing the economics of software development. What once required massive budgets and months of development can now be built faster and cheaper. And when you combine AI tools with an offshore development team, the economics become even harder to ignore. The irony? Many of the SaaS founders disagreeing with me probably built their own products using the very same business models that are now being disrupted. You used cheaper tools and resources to build your product. But when your customers discover they can do the same, suddenly it’s a problem? I’m not saying every SaaS product will disappear. I’m saying the days of charging ridiculous subscription fees simply because software is expensive to build are numbered. And if you can eliminate the middleman, why wouldn’t you at least consider it? Would you keep renting a house forever if building and owning one made more financial sense? The enterprise software industry needs to wake up.

posts.author: Lena Roufaeal
posts.headline: Technical Recruiter and People Partner | Talent Engineer | Career Advisor | Talent Acquisition Operations + University Recruiter
posts.text: There’s a lot of chatter about “engineers being rusty because of AI” as an explanation for weaker technical interview performance. I’ve used “rusty” myself, tbh 🥲 It feels plausible as SWEs are writing less code manually and AI now handles more implementation. I went back through several months of interview feedback to see what was behind the weakest performances. The recurring issue wasn’t usually forgotten syntax. Candidates struggled to make progress in unfamiliar code. They missed useful errors, skipped logs or docs, or got stuck without knowing what to inspect next. That’s debugging and it mattered long before Claude Code. I went down a research rabbit hole and found studies on expert vs novice debugging even going back to the 1980s. The theme was that stronger engineers are better at building a mental model, locating the real problem, gathering evidence, and adjusting their approach. Good debugging has never meant knowing everything from memory. The better question is, when you don’t know something, do you know how to make progress? Now this is where I think the “AI rust” conversation loses nuance because a few different things are actually happening: • Skill formation - you never got enough reps to build the skill deeply. • Skill decay - you built it, but practice it less because AI handles more of the work. • Fatigue - you still have the skill, but spend more time reviewing and correcting generated output. • Masking - you were never a strong debugger and AI covers that weakness for longer. That last one is the hypothesis I keep coming back to lately. A good coding agent can get someone unstuck repeatedly but makes the weakness stays hidden until something breaks or the engr can't collaborate effectively bec they can't explain/defend the work. I don’t think we have enough evidence to say AI is creating weak debuggers. But it can make weak diagnostic habits harder to see which really matters in hiring! This really changes how I partner with engineering leaders on interview design. If a team wants to measure code comprehension, debugging instincts, and independent reasoning, an AI-free exercise still gives useful signal. It’s not outdated! If we want to measure how someone works with AI, we need a different exercise. Give them the agent and watch how they scope the work, challenge the output, verify the result etc. Those are different signals. This is where I think technical recruiters have a bigger role to play now more than ever (and the work I enjoy the most): looking at interview data, finding patterns, translating them into clearer hiring signals, and working with engr leaders to build a better process around what we need to measure. Honestly, I think future engineering interviews will need both independent and AI-enabled signal, and I’m excited to help teams figure out what that looks like!

posts.text: I bumped into this young bobcat on my local mountain bike trail recently - first time I've seen one of these beautiful creatures out in the wild. The pic is a little fuzzy because it was late in the day and my iphone struggled to focus on its natural camouflage. I gave it some time to run off the trail before I continued, keeping an eye out for a protective parental unit - I had a feeling that mom was nearby. Watching this young one on the trail, learning how to make its way in the world got me thinking about some of the bright young talent that I've hired and coached over the years. These days I see junior engineers becoming demoralized as attention shifts toward AI. People who still have important work to do are starting to feel secondary to the tools and recent computer science grads are struggling to find their first jobs. The shift to AI means, at least in theory, that we can do more with less people, but if we stop hiring junior engineers because AI can do their work, where will our next senior engineers come from? Our senior engineers will eventually move on. Some will retire. Others will take different roles outside your company. Who will be ready to replace them and how do we prevent the loss of their critical domain knowledge? Junior engineers need opportunities to work through problems, learn from experienced colleagues and take on increasing responsibility. Building software is part of that development, but so is learning how to dive deep into requirements, troubleshoot a production issue, handle oncall operations and work with engineers across team/org boundaries to get things done. I’ve spent years building engineering teams, developing leaders and coaching/mentoring junior talent to take on increasingly complex and impactful work. If AI changes the work juniors can contribute, we need to rethink how we develop them. For engineering leaders, this should be part of our AI adoption plan. We still need to hire and develop the people who will lead what comes next. Your thoughts?

posts.text: The median Anthropic employee spends 20% more time in meetings than a year ago. Even technical individual contributors spend 16% more time in meetings. Anthropic published a report last week on how work has changed inside the company. They put it together from their own data: hiring, calendars and Slack. It's no secret Anthropic has grown a lot, and that's probably a big part of the spike in meetings. But I think another part is that as you create more and move faster, getting aligned becomes even more important. Many of the other numbers point the same way: ↳ Interactive Claude sessions spend around 80% of their time sitting idle, waiting for a human to respond. One engineer put it as people "bottlenecking the agents." ↳ Meta-work, which is basically setting up and keeping an eye on agents instead of doing the task yourself, went from 10% of the average employee's Claude sessions in fall 2025 to 22% in spring 2026. In an April survey, 20% of employees said their role shifted from doing work to managing Claudes, and one engineer said it feels like facing "an army of Claudes, with every one asking for my attention." ↳ There are around 17 engineers for every PM now, and that ratio's gone up since 2025. The share of people on technical teams who aren't actively coding fell by almost half, and commits from managers doubled. ↳ On hiring, juniors went from 27% of technical hires to 9%, and junior roles are just 6% of technical openings now. Around a third of ML managers and a fifth of software engineering managers said they're hiring less because of AI. ↳ Agents show up in nearly half of active public Slack channels. The report calls private work in DMs and unlogged meetings "invisible, confusing and discouraged," and one researcher said "leaders have to defend feedback out in the open." One non-technical employee said "that 20% that was strategic becomes 90% of the job." My read is that AI made a lot of the work cheap. What's scarce now is people's attention and judgment, plus the trust you still build face to face in all those extra meetings, which is basically the job leaders already had. Somebody has to decide which agent output gets a human read, because nobody can read all of it. Somebody has to figure out where judgment comes from when way fewer junior employees get hired, and even the authors admit none of their fixes "directly address the slowdown in junior hires." And since agents only know about decisions that get written down, feedback that used to live in a DM needs a more public home, which I'd guess many leaders find uncomfortable. And to be clear, Anthropic is not a normal company. They build frontier models and use them daily; the company tripled in size in the last year, and the authors say many of its employment practices can't be replicated across the economy. Still, it's the clearest look I've seen at what happens when agents do a lot of the work. And most of what got harder is the people stuff.

posts.text: 🚀 We are hiring: Trainee Engineer - Antenna Design WaveLink Technologies (Private) Limited is looking for an enthusiastic, driven Trainee Engineer to join our technical team in Islamabad. If you are a recent graduate with a passion for RF engineering and practical exposure to antenna design and simulation, this is your opportunity to build your career alongside experienced industry professionals. Position Overview * Role: Trainee Engineer - Antenna Design * Job Type: Full-time * Location: Islamabad (On-site) * Education: BE / BS in Electrical or Electronics Engineering Key Responsibilities * Modeling, simulation, and performance optimization of antenna structures across target frequency bands. * Utilize full-wave electromagnetic (EM) simulation software to analyze parameters such as return loss (S11), radiation patterns, gain, and impedance matching. * Support hardware prototyping, fabrication, tuning, and benchtop testing using RF laboratory equipment. * Document design iterations, test data, and technical findings to support ongoing product development. Requirements & Qualifications * Education: Bachelor’s degree in Electrical/Electronics Engineering (Fresh graduates or up to 1 year of experience). * Technical Knowledge: Strong theoretical foundation in electromagnetics, transmission lines, RF principles, and antenna theory (microstrip patch, dipoles, arrays, etc.). * Hands-on Experience: Practical exposure to antenna design through a Final Year Project (FYP), academic research, or previous internship. * Software Proficiency: Familiarity with EM simulation tools such as Ansys HFSS, CST Studio Suite, or Keysight ADS. * Lab Skills: Familiarity with RF test instruments (Vector Network Analyzers, Spectrum Analyzers, Signal Generators) is a plus. * Attributes: Proactive attitude, analytical problem-solving skills, and a strong drive to learn emerging wireless and RF technologies.
